item.content:encoded:
Third base wasn't viewed as a strong position entering 2026, and it doesn't look much stronger. Sure, we had players like Sal Stewart, Miguel Vargas, and Kevin McGonigle breaking out and establishing themselves as the next generation of the position, perhaps, and that ain't nothing.
But we also had deeply disappointing seasons from Jose Ramirez, Jazz Chisholm, Manny Machado, Austin Riley, Maikel Garcia, Bo Bichette, Eugenio Suarez, and Noelvi Marte, all of whom were drafted in the top 10 at the position. It would not be an overstatement to say that eight of the top 10 at the position busted, and you can throw Matt Chapman (3B12 in ADP) and Addison Barger (3B14) in there, too, to round it out.
So, yeah, we needed the breakouts. Because a lot of the old standbys let us down and it's not like the breakouts are without their flaws or concerns – any player who has only done it once is going to enter the next season with at least some question marks. Looking ahead to 2027, Junior Caminero might be the only sure thing at the position. He's going to be a first-rounder no matter what, but if you're the type to play position scarcity games, you might need to make sure you reach for him no matter where you're picking. Because if not, you're going to be left with a big question mark at an important position.
The toughest players to rank at third base
Jose Ramirez, Guardians
There are those who will argue Ramirez is very easy to rank. Some will say you should take his decline at face value; when a 34-year-old starts to fall off, they don't generally get it back. Ramirez enters the final week of the season hitting .237, his worst mark since 2015, while his 12 homers are his fewest since 2016. Sure, there was a mid-season hand surgery to blame it on, but to reiterate an earlier point: You probably shouldn't expect a 34-year-old to be healthier than he was in the past. Just take the numbers and the decline at face value.
That's one approach you can take. But I don't think it'll be mine. Because, despite the mediocre production, it doesn't actually look like Ramirez's skill set has declined much at all. His strikeout rate is up, but at 12.9%, it's still within a percentage point of his career mark, while his walk rate is actually his highest since 2021. His .306 wOBA is his worst mark since 2015, but his .329 expected wOBA is basically right in line with what he did in 2024, when he hit 39 homers and had arguably his best season ever. It's down from 2025, but not so much that it looks like a total collapse of the skill set. Ramirez still makes a ton of contact and he still hits the ball in the air to the pull side as often as anyone, the primary way he has overcome middling quality of contact metrics throughout his career.
Now, I'll grant that it's possible that the small, almost imperceptible changes in Ramirez's underlying skills have more impact than you might expect. Ramirez has been an outlier in how he outruns his underlying metrics, but that can be a delicate dance to keep up; Marcus Semien was an elite Fantasy player with a very similar skill set right up until the point he lost it. The margin for error with this kind of skill set might just be narrower than for guys who can crush the ball consistently, so maybe Ramirez's decline won't be stopped by a healthy offseason.
I'm open to that. He won't be a top-five player in my overall rankings for 2027. But he'll definitely still be a top-five third baseman, and might still be the second option off the board for me.
Miguel Vargas, White Sox
I don't think it's tough to figure out where Vargas ranks among third basemen. He belongs no lower than fourth, and I think you can make an extremely compelling case that only Junior Caminero should be ahead of him. So this might be more about just making sure everyone is prepared for the possibility that Vargas will be a second-round pick in 2027. The level he has reached in 2026 is completely unprecedented for Vargas, who has been playing pretty regularly since the second half of 2024 and had never really shown this kind of difference-making upside. But his .366 wOBA is actually a mild underperformance relative to his .381 expected wOBA, which is actually tied for the fifth-best mark of any hitter in the league.
I don't think Vargas is actually a top-five hitter in baseball. But if you wanted to argue he was a top-10 Fantasy option after this season, I wouldn't have a strong argument against it; the best argument I could muster is just, "Well, he's only done it once." But in addition to the underlying numbers, here's the other thing I love about what we're seeing from Vargas: He just refuses to slow down. July was the worst month of his season, but he responded with a .948 OPS in August, and then he went out and won AL Player of the Week last week. He's hitting .260/.373/.467 in the second half with strong plate discipline and plenty of speed and power.
Those gaudy underlying numbers are a little worse than they were early in the season, which might portend some regression in 2027. But, again, it probably wouldn't be reasonable to expect him to be a top-10 hitter again. But that doesn't mean the breakout isn't real, and where you rank him among Ramirez and Sal Stewart will mostly come down to personal preference. I imagine all three will be at least top-30 picks for me.
Manny Machado, Padres
There was a period in 2026 where Machado looked like himself again, and I was ready to write his slow start off as just that. He started hitting for real power again in June, and then in July he hit .292/.369/.552, putting the miserable start to the season behind him. But despite hitting three homers in his first five games back from the All-Star break, Machado enters the final week with just nine homers in 59 games since the break, while hitting .242/.331/.388 in the second half overall. If he deserved some benefit of the doubt for the slow start, it's hard to keep extending that when he came crashing back to earth over the final two months.
Machado's .330 xwOBA is definitely better than his actual .311 mark. However, it's still his worst since Statcast tracking began, and unlike Ramirez, he doesn't have a consistent track record of overcoming his underlying stats. There's still room for some improvement in 2027, most notably with his batting average, as a .234 BABIP isn't likely to sustain. But if he hits to his .244 xBA instead, that's still a drag on your average. Think about it this way: How excited have you been to have Nolan Arenado in your lineup this season? He hasn't been awful, but he hasn't been worth near the kind of price we've gotten used to paying for Machado. Neither is Machado at this point.
Kazuma Okamoto, Blue Jays
It's been an extremely successful first major-league season for Okamoto, though not necessarily in the way anyone expected. Okamoto was supposed to bring a contact-forward skill set, with just enough power to be a potential all-around impact hitter. Instead, he's been a pretty all-or-nothing power bat, hitting .235/.310/.459 with 33 homers and 89 RBI heading into the second half of the season. A longtime elite contact hitter in Japan, Okamoto has struck out 29% of the time and posted a 14% swinging-strike rate, both bottom-15 marks among qualifiers.
The strikeout issues got a little better in the second half, though he was a sub-.700 OPS bat in July and August before getting really hot in September, so it's hard to argue there's too much momentum building here. It's not unreasonable to expect a bit better from Okamoto with a full season under his belt, but the swing and miss issues on display were worrisome enough that he might just never get past it. Draft him for what he did in 2026, and if you get a .260 average from him instead, that'll be a huge win. But there are enough red flags in this profile that there's a real risk he'll end up being exposed before long.
Curtis Mead, Red Sox
Mead comes with all the typical questions of a one-season breakout, except he didn't even get the chance to do it for a full season. He platooned for part of the early part of the season and then suffered a fractured wrist in his very first game after being traded to the Red Sox in July. When he played, he was terrific, putting up a .253/.353/.498 line and more than holding his own against righties, so the case is pretty similar to that of Vargas as a former top prospect who finally made good. Only he did it for about half as many plate appearances, which makes it inherently more difficult to trust. I mean, just look at Michael Busch, who fully broke out in 2025 and had the underlying data to back it up, but then regressed badly in 2026. That doesn't mean the same thing will happen to Mead (or to Vargas, for that matter), but there's real regression risk that should keep his price down. I still think Mead deserves to be ranked as a top-10 third baseman, but I don't think he'll be worth drafting until at least the double-digit rounds.
Zack Gelof, Athletics
This feels like we're all Charlie Brown and we're gonna run up and try to kick that football again. Gelof has had a pretty awesome season, hitting 19 homers and stealing 14 bases in 105 games, while putting up a very solid .252/.314/.456 line. He has cut his strikeout rate to 25%, the best mark of his career, and while his underlying numbers don't quite back it up, his home park in Sacramento could help explain why it might not be unsustainable.
But we did this with Gelof after his rookie season. We overlooked scary plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues because he was a young, exciting hitter with a power-speed combo, and that was worth betting on. And I'm just not sure I want to make that mistake again. He's a pretty good athlete, but that doesn't really translate into much more than above-average raw power, and I just don't have much faith that's enough to overcome what are still some pretty scary issues under the hood. Gelof has, to his credit, become a more patient hitter, though not necessarily a more discerning one; his chase rate has dropped about as much as his in-zone swing rate has. He still has big swing-and-miss issues, and it just always feels like Gelof is going to be dancing on a knife's edge. If he's still there after the first 150 picks or so, I might be willing to take a chance on him. I just don't think I can bring myself to rank Gelof as a starting-caliber player in most leagues.

We’ve made it to the final week of the regular season. There are still two divisions in the American League up for grabs, a couple of long-shot playoff hopefuls looking to make a last-minute run, and playoff seeding to fight over. It should make for a dramatic end to a great season.
Our power rankings use a modified Elo rating system. If you’re familiar with chess rankings, you’ll know that Elo is an elegant ranking format that measures teams’ relative strength and is very reactive to recent performance. To avoid overweighting recent results during the season, we weigh each team’s raw Elo rank using our coin flip playoff odds (specifically, we regress the playoff odds by 50% and weigh those against the raw Elo ranking, increasing in weight as the season progresses to a maximum of 25%). The weighted Elo ranks are then displayed as “Power Score” in the tables below. As the best and worst teams sort themselves out between now and October, they’ll filter to the top and bottom of the rankings, while the exercise remains reactive to hot streaks and cold snaps. If you’re looking for a visual representation of the ups and downs of your team throughout the season, look no further than the brand new Power Rankings Board in the FanGraphs Lab.
First up are the full rankings, presented in a sortable table. Below that, I’ve grouped the teams into tiers with comments on a handful of clubs. You’ll notice that the official ordinal rankings don’t always match the tiers — there are times where I take editorial liberties when grouping teams together — but generally, the ordering is consistent. It was a great week for the Brewers. They won their fourth straight NL Central title and sixth in the last nine years, and also set another franchise record for wins in a single season, one year after setting the previous record. They now have a chance to win 100 games for the first time in club history this week and still have the top seed in the NL to play for.
The Rays swept the Athletics and won their series against the Red Sox last week to put some distance between themselves and the Yankees in the AL East race. The gap in the division is now six games, and even though the two rivals play each other four times during the final week of the season, it would take a massive collapse from Tampa Bay to upset the current standings. Because the Rays also currently lead the season series with the Yankees, 6-3, all they need is to win one of the four games in New York to take the division title. With Shane McClanahan still recovering from his forearm injury — his availability for the playoffs is up in the air — Freddy Peralta has stepped up to lead the pitching staff over the last few weeks. Across his last five starts, he’s allowed just three runs in 28 2/3 innings. That’s the kind of production the Rays were hoping to get when they acquired him at the trade deadline.

The Dodgers are getting all their pieces in place for the postseason. Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki will be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and Shohei Ohtani should follow on Wednesday. There’s a lingering question about Blake Snell’s status after he injured his groin last week, but it sounds like he’ll be able to make a start during the final weekend of the season. And even though the majority of the year has been a slog for Kyle Tucker, his bat seems to have finally woken up at the right time; he collected nine hits and three home runs last week.
Having won 13 of their last 14 games, the Padres are peaking at exactly the right moment. They’ve surged five games ahead of the Diamondbacks and one ahead of the Phillies in the NL Wild Card standings, and are now tied with the Cubs for the top spot. San Diego’s final series of the season against Arizona still looms large, especially if the Friars stumble against the Dodgers in the series beforehand. You’re probably familiar with Fernando Tatis Jr.’s hot streak — he blasted four home runs last week to bring his total in September up to eight — but the biggest contributor to the Padres’ success recently has been Ty France. He had 12 hits and a home run last week and has posted a fantastic 168 wRC+ during the second half of the season.
After a couple of years away from the top, the Braves are NL East champions again — it’s their seventh division title in the last nine years. Atlanta’s dominance this year has been a welcome return to form. Even though his season has been a bit up and down, Ronald Acuña Jr. is looking like the superstar that won the MVP back in 2023 again. Last week, he smacked three home runs, including a go-ahead grand slam on Saturday, and is running a 191 wRC+ in September.
A little more than a week after being activated off the IL, Aaron Judge is back on the shelf, this time with a calf injury sustained on Wednesday. His availability for the playoffs is still up in the air, though he’s confident that he’ll be able to return sooner rather than later. Thankfully, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and there’s some confidence that Trent Grisham will also be ready to return for the postseason. It helps that Ben Rice has bounced back from a rough August to post a 192 wRC+ in September. Still, Judge’s injury is a major blow to the Yankees’ hopes for a deep October run.

Even though the Red Sox lost both of their series last week, they managed to clinch a postseason berth on Sunday. It’s the cap to a remarkable turnaround after the team looked completely lost in mid-June. Boston can officially secure the second Wild Card spot with a couple of wins against the Guardians this week. Then the team can turn its attention to the Yankees and the rematch of last year’s Wild Card matchup between these two historic rivals.
Nothing is going to come easy for the Phillies over the next few weeks. The team placed Jesús Luzardo on the IL last week with a shoulder injury, but thankfully, it sounds like he’ll be ready to pitch in the playoffs. But before they count their chickens, they need to actually clinch a playoff spot. Philadelphia is four games up on the Diamondbacks in the NL Wild Card race, but its upcoming opponents are no cake walk; the Phillies have the Brewers and Rays on the schedule to finish off the regular season. Facing two of the best teams in baseball is quite a test ahead of the postseason, and the Phillies haven’t exactly been playing well lately.
The biggest concern for the Cubs right now is the status of Alex Bregman. He was struck by a foul ball in the face while standing in the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game and was taken to the hospital for further evaluation. Alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bregman has been one of the best hitters in baseball since the All-Star break. It would be a huge blow if the third baseman had to miss any significant amount of time at this point in the season. As for Crow-Armstrong, he’s two stolen bases away from joining the 40/40 club. He put a few finishing touches on his MVP case last week by bopping four more home runs, bringing his season total up to 45.

There was some upheaval in the two division races represented in this tier. Entering last week one game behind the White Sox in the AL Central standings, the Guardians took two of three games against the South Siders in a dramatic series, which included a walk-off on Tuesday and an improbable go-ahead homer on Wednesday. From there, although Chicago took advantage of playing — and winning — on Thursday while Cleveland was off to pull back into a tie atop the division, the Guardians just kept winning, sweeping the the Athletics over the weekend to bring their winning streak to five. José Ramírez finally broke out of his extended slump, tallying nine hits, a home run, and four stolen bases last week.
As for the White Sox, they won three of their four games against the the Tigers, but that one loss was enough to drop them to a game behind Cleveland in the Central. Still, the Sox have a three-game cushion for the final AL Wild Card spot, and they own the tiebreaker over the Guardians, meaning both first place and a potential first-round bye are still in their sights. Miguel Vargas is carrying most of the load for the lineup right now, hitting three home runs last week, but he needs some support if Chicago wants to make some noise in the postseason.
Over in the AL West, the Astros were swept by the Braves this past weekend, allowing the Rangers to jump into first place with a .500 record. Texas enters this week one game up, but crucially Houston holds the tiebreaker. If the Rangers can manage to hang on, it would be just their second postseason appearance in the last decade. The last time they made the playoffs, they won the World Series.
The Houston bullpen was responsible for the backbreaking losses on Saturday and Sunday, but the lack of offense has been a much bigger problem. Over the Astros’ last 10 games, they’ve scored more than four runs in a game just once. Yordan Alvarez looked fine last week (eight hits, including two home runs) after his ankle scare the previous weekend, and Jeremy Peña has been great too (10 hits, three homers), but the rest of the lineup has been struggling. During this 10-game stretch, Houston hitters not named Alvarez or Peña have combined for an ugly 55 wRC+.

The first victory was a walk-off and the second was highlighted by a go-ahead grand slam from Nolan Arenado. Arizona needs to take care of business in Colorado and get some help from the Dodgers to ensure that the final series against the Padres has some stakes. There’s a chance the Phillies could crash out, opening another window for the Snakes, but the direct path is through San Diego.
The Blue Jays’ hopes for a last-minute surge into the playoffs were dashed last week when they lost both of their series to the Tigers and Rangers. They’re three games back and have the Astros to contend with if they want to try and sneak into that final Wild Card spot. It’s probably too little, too late, but the team is activating Trey Yesavage off the IL on Monday as one more reinforcement ahead of a final push.

The series between the Orioles and Mets last week in Queens turned out to be more interesting than you’d expect from two teams mired in hugely disappointing seasons. Pete Alonso made his first appearance as a member of the opposing team at Citi Field and wound up hitting his 300th career home run on Tuesday, a game-tying shot in the ninth inning. He received a huge ovation from the hometown crowd, which drew some irksome comments from a few Mets players and staff after the game. Baltimore wound up sweeping New York to cut its deficit in the AL Wild Card race to 2.5 games. Alas, a sweep by the Brewers over the weekend slammed the door shut on any playoff hopes the O’s still had.
Even though the Marlins’ season essentially ended with that 12-game losing streak back in July, they have made some significant progress in their quest to become a contending club. Otto Lopez looks like a star they can build the lineup around, while Eury Pérez and Max Meyer should be strong enough to anchor the pitching staff in the years ahead. There’s also a cohort of young prospects in the upper minors who should be making their debuts soon. The future in Miami is brighter than it’s been in a while.
This is the huge step forward the Reds were hoping to see from Elly De La Cruz. In September, he has blasted seven home runs, including in five straight games earlier this month, and is running a major league-best 236 wRC+. It’s too bad the rest of Cincinnati’s roster is a bit of a mess. Sal Stewart has been excellent as De La Cruz’s sidekick, but the starting rotation has struggled mightily, and the big injury to Hunter Greene has thrown the ceiling of that group up in the air heading into next year. Still, building around a superstar like De La Cruz should make things easier if the resources to improve the rest of the roster are made available.

The AL Central crown runs through Kansas City; both the White Sox and Guardians travel to face the Royals during the final week of the season. Unfortunately, the Royals haven’t been playing well enough recently to act as a spoiler. They ended August with a 13-3 stretch, but they’ve been the worst team in the AL in September, with just five wins in 18 games.
It took a lot longer than expected, but the Twins were finally eliminated from the playoff race last week. It was a drama-filled week, too. They won a wild extra-inning walk-off affair against the Yankees on Wednesday and then were walked-off twice against the Angels between two shutout victories over the weekend. Even though they all made their big league debuts over the last few weeks, Walker Jenkins, Kaelen Culpepper, and Emmanuel Rodriguez never all appeared in a game together. That trio represents the future of the organization, so it’s a little disappointing that that future couldn’t be realized in a small way this year.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] What to watch for in the final week of American League play
item.dc:creator: Andrés Chávez
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays, the New York Yankees, and the Boston Red Sox have all punched their ticket to the postseason. item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays, the New York Yankees, and the Boston Red Sox have all punched their ticket to the postseason. With the final week of the 2026 MLB regular season already upon us, several other American League squads are playing for a place in October, too.
Even the Rays and Yankees technically have to decide who wins the AL East, with the former enjoying a hefty advantage heading into the final week, needing just one win over the Bombers to secure it. After that, there are two wide-open divisions and an exciting competition for the last Wild Card spot.
Here’s where every team stands in the race:
Tampa Bay Rays
Remaining games: 4 @ Yankees, 3 @ Phillies
Current record: 95-60
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL East (6 games ahead of NYY)
Final week outlook: The Rays have been, far and away, the top team in the American League by win-loss record, and unless something really crazy happens, they will enter the postseason with a first-round bye and wait for the winner of the battle between the top two Wild Cards—the Yankees and Red Sox—in the Division Series. They’ll still try to play competitive games after clinching, as they certainly wouldn’t say no to having home-field advantage over NL teams in a potential World Series matchup* as they seek their first championship in franchise history, but the pressure this week is much lighter.
*We’re keeping the focus on the AL in this post, but for those curious, Tampa Bay’s 95-60 record currently trails the Dodgers’ 96-60 and the Brewers’ 98-58. Atlanta trails at 92-64. The Dodgers have the Padres and Giants to end 2026 while the Brewers have the Phillies and Cardinals, and the Braves have the Reds and Marlins.
New York Yankees
Remaining games: 4 vs. Rays, 3 vs. Orioles
Current record: 89-66
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 2nd in AL East (6 games behind TB); 1st in Wild Card race (5.5 games ahead of 2nd Wild Card spot, held by BOS)
Final week outlook: Unless they sweep the Rays and Orioles, the Yankees virtually have no chance of winning the AL East crown. Instead, they will likely enter the postseason as the top Wild Card team, as they have a healthy cushion over the Red Sox, their likely foe in the Wild Card round. The odds of that series being at Fenway rather than Yankee Stadium are extremely low, especially since New York has the tiebreaker over Boston.
Boston Red Sox
Remaining games: 3 vs. Guardians, 3 vs. Cubs
Current record: 84-72
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 3rd in AL East, 2nd in Wild Card race (5.5 games behind NYY for top WC spot, 4 games ahead of CHW, owners of the 3rd WC spot)
Final week outlook: The Red Sox are highly unlikely to move from the second AL Wild Card spot, since they have a four-game cushion over the White Sox, owners of the third slot, and are 5.5 games behind the Yanks for the top one. They’ve been all but locked into this spot for awhile now and just clinched their playoff berth yesterday with Houston’s loss to Atlanta.
Cleveland Guardians
Remaining games: 3 @ Red Sox, 3 @ Royals
Current record: 81-75
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL Central (1 game ahead of CHW)
Final week outlook: Eyeing their third consecutive division title and seventh since 2016, the Guardians are currently one game up in the race for the AL Central, but need to avoid a tie with the White Sox at the top because Chicago owns the tiebreaker. Cleveland is peaking at the right time, though, and José Ramírez is finally starting to show some signs of a breakthrough at the plate. If that’s the case, they will be dangerous with a strong young core and two aces at the top: AL strikeout leader Gavin Williams and Rookie of the Year contender Parker Messick. Second baseman Travis Bazzana isn’t too shabby of a rookie, either.
Chicago White Sox
Remaining games: 3 @ Royals, 3 vs. Rockies
Current record: 80-76
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 2nd in AL Central (1 game behind CLE), 3rd in Wild Card race (3 games ahead of HOU and TOR, 5 ahead of BAL)
Final week outlook: Chicago’s lack of quality starting pitching seems to have caught up to them in September, but they are still a dangerous team that is trending towards its first postseason appearance since 2021. They have a chance to win the AL Central: all they need to do is finish in at least a tie with the Guardians, and though both the Pale Hose and Guards will face the Royals this week, the Southsiders have an easier other foe in the Rockies. Remember, winning the division would likely even give Chicago the second seed in the AL and a first-round bye to face the victor of the AL West/last Wild Card matchup.
It’s already been an improbably great season for the White Sox, as merely getting a winning season would’ve been a huge success for a team that lost a modern record 121 games in 2024 and 102 last year. But missing out at this point would still be quite the disappointment.
Texas Rangers
Remaining games: 3 vs. Mets, 3 @ Twins
Current record: 78-78
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL West (1 game ahead of HOU)
Final week outlook: If the Rangers finish with more wins than the Astros, they will capture the AL West despite their thoroughly mediocre record (the Mariners’ deeply disappointing 2026 really made the division a mess). It’s a key week in Texas, as the range of outcomes is wide: they could win the division and finish as high as the second seed if they can best the AL Central champ’s line; they could be the final Wild Card squad, or they could miss the playoffs entirely for the third year in a row since winning it all in 2023 behind two-time World Series MVP Corey Seager.
It’s important to note that the Rangers need to beat the Astros by at least one game to take the AL West crown because Houston owns the tiebreaker. The Rangers own tiebreakers against the Orioles, Guardians, and Blue Jays, and lost against the White Sox and, as explained, the Astros. The AL West winner is a near-lock to face the worst Wild Card team in the first round, though they will host the best-of-three.
Toronto Blue Jays
Remaining games: 3 @ Orioles, 3 vs. Reds
Current record: 77-79
Current position in division/Wild Card race: tied with HOU for 4th in Wild Card standings, 3 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: Last year’s AL champs can’t win their division: their only path to the playoffs is the third and final Wild Card spot. With that in mind, however, they would need to finish ahead of both the White Sox and the Rangers because both of them own the tiebreaker against Toronto. It sure doesn’t help that ace Dylan Cease was scratched from his next start and is undergoing an MRI.
The Jays tied the season series against Houston, which, in the event of a tie at the third WC spot between them, would take us to intra-divisional record to decide. There, Toronto is 25-24 against AL East opponents, and the Astros are 22-24 vs. AL West foes, presently giving the Jays the edge, though that could change this week since they both face intra-divisional rivals.
For what it’s worth, Toronto won the tiebreakers against the Guardians and the Orioles.
Houston Astros
Remaining games: 2 @ Mariners, 4 @ A’s
Current record: 77-79
Current position in division/Wild Card race: tied with TOR for 4th in Wild Card standings, 3 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: Much like the White Sox in the AL Central, the Astros are one game behind in their division and own the tiebreaker against the Rangers, so all they need to do is catch them by the end of the week. They have lost three straight, though, with a -59 run differential, so despite the best efforts of MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez, they aren’t particularly good. We have seen plenty of mediocre squads make it in the past, so they definitely have a chance — especially since they get to play the mostly-hapless M’s and A’s this week.
Houston can still qualify via the last Wild Card, but the division presents a smoother path. Since we’re running through them, they own tiebreakers vs. the White Sox, Guardians, and Rangers, losing vs. the Orioles and tying vs. Toronto.
Baltimore Orioles
Remaining games: 3 vs. Blue Jays, 3 @ Yankees
Current record: 75-81
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 6th in Wild Card standings, 5 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: At this point, the Orioles need a miracle to get in. They needed to sweep the Brewers this past weekend to put themselves in a position to compete. Instead, they got swept themselves. Baltimore won tiebreakers against the White Sox and the Astros, and lost against the Rangers, Guardians, and Blue Jays. But again, they have essentially no shot whatsoever. That final weekend series in the Bronx could’ve been interesting; alas.

The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

CLEVELAND -- - Gavin Williams threw seven shutout innings, Jo Adell had an RBI infield single and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Athletics 1-0 Sunday to remain atop the AL Central.
Steven Kwan added three hits for Cleveland, which posted its seventh series sweep of the season and third at home.
The Guardians (81-75) are one game in front of the Chicago White Sox, who defeated Detroit 8-1. They finish the season on the road with series against Boston and Kansas City.
Williams (14-8) gave up three hits and struck out nine to move into the American League lead with 244 strikeouts. Toronto's Dylan Cease is in second with 239. It is the 13th time in 31 starts this season that the right-hander has had at least nine strikeouts.
Cade Smith worked 1 1/3 innings for his 39th save in 44 opportunities.
The Athletics were swept for the second straight series and lost all six games on their road trip.
José Ramírez led off the fourth with a double down the right-field line, advanced to third on Chase DeLauter's fly out to left and scored on Jo Adell's infield single. Pitcher Jack Perkins (3-12) fielded the soft grounder on the grass in front of the mound, but his throw hit Adell in the back as he was in the basepath.
Athletics manager Mark Kotsay was ejected for the third time this season for agruing the call.
Perkins went six innings and allowed one run on four hits.
The Athletics' best chance came in the eighth inning when they had runners on second and third with one out. Hunter Gaddis struck out pinch-hitter Carlos Cortes and Smith whiffed Henry Bolte.
Up next
Athletics: Return home to face the Los Angeles Angels on Tuesday. LHP Brady Brasso (1-3, 4.50 ERA) will take the mound.
Guardians: LHP Parker Messic (12-9, 2.57 ERA) goes on Tuesday to start a three-game series at Boston.

La jugada que terminó por cambiar el rumbo del encuentro llegó en la quinta entrada. Los Diamondbacks habían conseguido llenar las bases frente al abridor de Nueva York, Will Warren, quien dejó el montículo para darle paso al relevista Brent Headrick.
El pitcher logró retirar a Geraldo Perdomo con un ponche para conseguir el segundo out, pero después vino el descontrol. Headrick otorgó una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll, situación que permitió que Arizona sumara una carrera y dejara las bases listas para Arenado.
Con cuenta de 2-1, el tercera base no perdonó. Arenado encontró el lanzamiento y mandó la pelota por encima de la barda para completar el grand slam y darle la vuelta al partido. Fue el noveno cuadrangular con las bases llenas de su carrera, además de que alcanzó al cubano Yordan Álvarez, de los Houston Astros, como líder de las Grandes Ligas en grand slams durante esta temporada.
Pero el poder ofensivo de Arizona no se limitó a Arenado. Perdomo también tuvo una tarde productiva al conectar un sencillo productor en la primera entrada y posteriormente un triple que llevó otra carrera al plato durante el séptimo episodio.
Los Yankees, por su parte, habían respondido con fuerza en el tercer inning. Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones conectaron cuadrangulares consecutivos dentro de esa entrada frente al abridor de Arizona, Corbin Burnes, para mantener con vida a Nueva York.
Sin embargo, la ofensiva neoyorquina se apagó después de ese episodio. El bullpen de Arizona tomó el control y, encabezado por Justin Martínez, consiguió limitar a los Yankees a solamente tres imparables durante las últimas 6 entradas. Martínez se apuntó la victoria, la tercera de su temporada, con marca de 3-0.

item.content:encoded:
After going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts in the first two games of this series, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had himself another big day in the third contest. PCA singled, doubled, homered and stole a base and helped lead the Cubs to a 9-1 blowout of the Reds, a victory tempered by a freak injury to Alex Bregman. More on the latter anon, first let’s wrap this win.
The Cubs got on the board in the first inning. PCA led off the game with a single and stole second, his 38th [VIDEO].
The Cubs extended their lead in the third. PCA led off with a double. A note on that double from BCB’s JohnW53:
With his third-inning double, Pete Crow-Armstrong has at least 30 homers, doubles and steals.
Only one Cub had done that before: PCA, last year.
Forty players on other teams have done it, 12 of them also multiple times. PCA is among 10 with two. Alfonso Soriano did it four times; Barry Bonds and Jose Ramirez, three.
It was noted on the Marquee broadcast that PCA’s 40-HR, 30-double, 30-steal year is the first ever by a MLB center fielder — nope, not Willie Mays, not Ken Griffey Jr., no one, until now. I’ve said it before, but don’t ever forget what you are seeing from Pete this year — it is truly historic.
Anyway, PCA then went to third on a ground out by Seiya Suzuki. The Cubs then loaded the bases on walks drawn by Michael Busch and Bregman.
Per the Marquee broadcast, that’s 22 bases-loaded walks for the Cubs this year, the most in MLB.
With the bases still loaded, Michael Conforto struck out, but Pedro Ramirez followed with a two-run single to make it 5-0 [VIDEO].
Now to the Bregman incident in the fourth inning. With two out, Busch hit a foul ball that struck Bregman, who was in the on-deck circle, in the face. Bregman immediately left the game and was replaced by Matt Shaw. Here’s what that looked like [VIDEO].
Per Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks, the ball hit Bregman in the cheekbone, which is swollen. There was also a facial cut, but we don’t know anything beyond that. Hopefully it’s not too serious and Bregman doesn’t have a concussion.
While all this was going on, David Peterson was sailing along, striking out seven over the first four innings. The Reds made it 5-1 on a solo homer by JJ Bleday in the fourth.
The Cubs got that run right back in the fifth on a solo homer by Michael Conforto, his 15th [VIDEO].
If you’re keeping track:
Kyle Tucker, 16 HR, 515 AB
Michael Conforto, 15 HR, 294 AB
That blast tied PCA with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. The Cubs also lead MLB in home runs with 217; as noted on the Marquee broadcast, the last time the Cubs led all of baseball in home runs was 1958, led by Ernie Banks with 47 in his first MVP season.
Peterson completed six innings, allowing three hits and just the one run on Bleday’s homer. Here are his seven strikeouts [VIDEO].
More on Peterson’s afternoon from BCB’s JohnW53:
David Peterson’s quality start was his fifth as a Cub, fourth most on the team. Shota Imanaga has 14, as many as the next two combined: Matthew Boyd, eight, and Colin Rea, six. Edward Cabrera and Jameson Taillon both have four. Five others have one to three.
Peterson could be a valuable weapon in the postseason, either as a starter or out of the bullpen.
The Cubs weren’t done homering, either. After Caleb Thielbar threw a scoreless seventh, Suzuki lofted his 25th into the batter’s eye to make it 9-1 [VIDEO].
More on recent Cubs home runs from John:
With their three home runs, the Cubs have hit nine in their last four games (three, one, two, three). They had hit 12 in their previous 14 games, since smacking a team-record nine at home vs. the Brewers on Aug. 31.
Edward Cabrera was given the eighth inning, a good low-leverage situation. He allowed a leadoff single and after retiring the next hitter, another Reds batter reached on an error by Ramirez. But Cabrera got Elly De La Cruz to hit into an inning-ending double play.
Colin Rea finished up with a 1-2-3 ninth, his first game action in 11 days, on just eight pitches. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
The Cubs will clinch a postseason berth if the Yankees defeat the Diamondbacks Sunday, a game that’s just begun at the time of this recap. The Padres, tied with the Cubs for the top wild card spot with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker, are playing the Marlins in a contest in San Diego that’s also just underway. The Phillies defeated the Mets Sunday, so the Cubs still lead Philadelphia by a game. Thanks to the Mets for taking two of the four games from the Phillies over the weekend.
The Cubs have Monday off, then open the final regular season home series Tuesday evening against the Marlins at Wrigley Field. Kevin Gausman will start for the Cubs and Janson Junk will go for Miami. Game time Tuesday is 6:40 p.m. CT and TV coverage will be via Marquee Sports Network.

item.content:encoded:
Some baseball dreams begin with the finest equipment, elite coaching and scouts waiting to spot the next big star. José Ramírez's journey began very differently. The Cleveland Guardians star grew up with limited resources, faced doubts about his potential and had to fight for recognition. Years later, he reached 1,000 career RBIs, turning an overlooked beginning into a remarkable MLB story.
José Ramírez's humble beginnings in the Dominican Republic
Long before thousands of fans cheered his name at Progressive Field, Ramírez was a young boy in Baní, a city in the Dominican Republic, trying to make the most of whatever baseball equipment he could find.
His family faced financial struggles, and even getting a proper glove was difficult. In a 2023 MLB feature, Ramírez recalled the challenges his family faced while he was growing up.
“It was difficult for my dad,” he said through interpreter Agustin Rivero. “He didn’t have much work, we didn’t have much money. I had to play with a glove that was too tight.”
That small detail offers a glimpse into the reality of Ramírez's early life. For him, baseball was never simply a game played for fun. It represented a chance to change his family's circumstances and build a future beyond the financial limits he knew as a child.
Before he began playing organised baseball, Ramírez and other neighbourhood children played Vitilla, a popular Dominican street game. They used plastic water jug caps as balls and sticks as bats. The makeshift equipment could not match what elite prospects used, but the children made the most of what they had.
Ramírez also faced a challenge that had nothing to do with money. His small frame made him easy to overlook in a sport where scouts often search for size, strength and physical potential.
Yet, the young infielder kept showing up and competing. His story was taking shape long before a Major League Baseball team gave him a chance.
MLB scouts overlooked José Ramírez despite his talent
Ramírez's road to professional baseball was anything but straightforward. While other young players attracted attention at showcases in the Dominican Republic, he often found himself waiting on the sidelines.
By the time he was 17, his chances of securing a professional contract appeared to be slipping away. Many of the top Dominican prospects signed with MLB teams at 16, leaving Ramírez behind as scouts focused on younger players with more conventional physical profiles.
He was frequently used as a fill-in at showcases rather than receiving the same opportunities as the headline prospects. His lack of size and limited scouting attention made it harder for him to stand out, even when his performance suggested he deserved a closer look.
Ramírez later described the doubts he faced in an ESPN interview, recalling how people judged him before he had the chance to prove himself.
“I knew it would be hard for me [to get signed] because [scouts] are always looking for a Mike Trout, a Bryce Harper. Those kind of guys; big, strong guys. I imagine that [José] Altuve had the same thing happen to him. I guess nobody believed Altuve could be what he has become. Sometimes your size, a smaller body, one does not attract attention or anything and nobody believes in you,” he said.
The lack of interest could have ended his dream before it truly began. Instead, Ramírez continued to play, trusting his ability even when the people evaluating him did not share that confidence.
His opportunity finally arrived in 2009. During a showcase, Cleveland's scouting director John Mirabelli and scout Ramón Peña watched him play second base. Ramírez delivered three hits that day, followed by three more the next day and five hits during a doubleheader.
Peña pushed for Cleveland to sign him. The Guardians' organisation, then known as the Indians, eventually offered Ramírez a $50,000 signing bonus.
It was a modest investment compared with the money given to highly sought-after international prospects. But that decision would become one of the most significant signings in the franchise's history.
José Ramírez turned a modest signing into an MLB career
Even after signing with Cleveland, Ramírez had no guarantee of becoming a major league star. His small signing bonus did not bring the same expectations or opportunities that came with a lucrative prospect contract.
He had to earn his place at every level, moving through the Dominican Summer League, the Arizona Rookie League and several other Minor League stops. There were no shortcuts. Each promotion required him to prove that his performance could translate against stronger competition.
Cleveland's front office later acknowledged that Ramírez did not arrive with the attention usually reserved for elite prospects. His progress came through steady work rather than early hype.
That gradual rise makes his career particularly striking. Ramírez developed into one of baseball's most consistent hitters, combining contact skills, speed, power and versatility. He also became a switch-hitter capable of putting pressure on opposing pitchers from either side of the plate.
His success challenged the assumptions that had limited his opportunities as a teenager. The traits that once made him easy to overlook did not prevent him from becoming a central figure in Cleveland's lineup.
Over time, Ramírez became far more than a promising player who exceeded expectations. He established himself as a franchise cornerstone, a perennial offensive threat and a player whose contributions extended well beyond individual statistics.
The journey also reflects the importance of the people who believed in him early. Peña continued to advocate for Ramírez when others saw little reason to invest in him. That faith gave the young Dominican infielder an opening, but Ramírez still had to turn it into a career.
José Ramírez reaches 1,000 career RBIs with the Guardians
On September 18, 2026, Ramírez added another defining moment to his career. The Guardians star crushed a solo home run against the Athletics at Progressive Field, recording his 1,000th career RBI during Cleveland's 5-3 victory.
The milestone came in the sixth inning, with his 401-foot blast giving the home crowd another reason to celebrate a player who had spent years earning their admiration.
Ramírez became just the second player in Cleveland franchise history to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Earl Averill. He also became the 12th active MLB player to reach the mark.
For a player who once struggled to attract the attention of scouts, the achievement carries a special meaning. It reflects years of consistency, development and the ability to deliver when his team needs him.
Guardians manager Stephen Vogt captured the scale of the accomplishment by putting it in perspective.
“I like to use those round numbers,” Vogt said. “[It’s] 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?”
Ramírez, however, remained focused on the team's success rather than his personal achievement.
“Thank God for the opportunity to play here for this organization and be able to achieve [1,000 RBIs],” Ramírez said through team interpreter Agustin Rivero. “But most important is that we're able to win today, because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
That mindset helps explain why Ramírez's story resonates beyond the milestone itself. His journey is about more than proving scouts wrong. It is about turning a difficult start into a career built on persistence, consistency and loyalty to the game.
From a young boy playing with an ill-fitting glove in Baní to one of Cleveland's most accomplished hitters, José Ramírez has shown that a player's beginning does not have to define his ceiling. His 1,000th RBI is another chapter in a story that is still being written.
Reporting note: The career milestone and game details are based on MLB's September 19, 2026, report. The early-life details are drawn from MLB's 2023 profile and ESPN's reporting on Ramírez's rise.

item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

If there's one thing that Jose Ramirez has been known for throughout his career, it's how consistent he has been as the Cleveland Guardians star. Year in and year out, Ramirez is an MVP candidate in the American League.
Unfortunately, the 2026 season has been a different story for Ramirez.
The superstar's stats are nowhere near on par with his typical career numbers. There could be several reasons for this, but one of the primary ones has to do with the hamstring injury Ramirez suffered in the middle of June.
Even though Ramirez only missed a little over a month with the injury, he still hasn't looked like the same hitter. Even though it's normal for a player returning from this injury to take time to regain their power, it's still been weird to see Ramirez struggle so much at the plate.
Even though the season numbers aren't there for Ramirez, what the Guardians can fall back on is his stats over the last few weeks.
It really looks like Ramirez has turned a corner and is regaining his form just in time for the final playoff push.
Ramirez has logged six hits in his last seven games, including a pair of doubles in the rubber match against the Chicago White Sox and a solo blast against the Athletics, which gave him his 1,000th career RBI.
Ramirez admitted that his recovery from the hamate injury is still a work in progress, but there have certainly been days when he's felt much better.
"Working on it everyday," said Ramirez through his interpreter Auggie Rivero.
"I have to keep working on the training room every day because this is the type of injury, one day you feel good, the next one doesn't feels so well... The last couple days I feel better, but we know this type of injury can just vary every day."
Manager Stephen Vogt acknowledged after Friday's win that Ramirez hasn't felt like the same player since coming back from injury, but has still made an impact on this team by leading by example in the locker room.
"As he was coming back, and we had to give him off days. He was not happy about it," Vogt said.
"He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day, and we know there are days when he is not feeling well, and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day. It's just such a great example for young guys to see that just because you're not feeling 100 percent doesn't mean you can't go out and contribute to help the team win."
Cleveland's offense has been hot and cold at times this season, but if the Guardians are truly getting vintage Ramirez back for a potential playoff run, this could become one of the more dangerous teams in baseball come October.

As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

CLEVELAND -- - José Ramírez and rookie Travis Bazzana homered and Joey Cantillo pitched six scoreless innings as the Cleveland Guardians rallied to beat the Athletics 5-3 on Friday night and stay atop the AL Central.
Ramírez connected in the sixth inning to give the Guardians a two-run cushion. His 12th homer was also the seven-time All-Star's 1,000th RBI, making him just the second Cleveland player to reach the plateau. Earl Averill drove in 1,084 runs.
Bazzana snapped a 3-3 tie in the fifth as the Guardians came back after falling behind 3-0 in the first.
Cleveland, 18-9 since Aug. 20, came in tied with Chicago for first in the division. The White Sox hold the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Cantillo (10-9) allowed two hits in six innings after replacing opener Daniel Espino. Cantillo has not given up a run in 10 innings over his past two outings.
Hunter Gaddis and Cade Smith finished off the combined three-hitter. Smith worked the ninth for his 38th save.
Zack Gelof hit a three-run homer for the A's, who are 0-4 on their final road trip of 2026.
Bazzana put Cleveland ahead 4-3 in the fifth with his 15th homer, a 411-foot leadoff drive to center off Scott Blewett (2-1).
The Guardians had squandered early scoring chances, loading the bases in the first two innings but failing to push a run across.
Cleveland finally strung some hits together in the fourth, scoring three times off starter Mason Barnett to tie it.
Rocchio, who leads all MLB No. 9 hitters in RBI with 50, delivered a two-run double and scored on Ramírez's two-out single.
Espino opened for Cleveland and started poorly.
The right-hander walked three in the first and allowed the three-run homer to Gelof, his 19th.

CLEVELAND -- As the Progressive Field crowd roared around him, José Ramírez paused and leaned back in the left-handed batter’s box to admire his work. There was no doubt where the baseball he launched to right field was headed.
That image has played on repeat over the past 14 seasons. This time, it came with a heavy dose of history, and it was well-timed as the Guardians continue to push for the postseason.
Ramírez tallied his 1,000th career RBI on Friday by launching his 297th career home run, in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ matchup with the A’s in the opener of a three-game series. The superstar third baseman joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone.
The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win. They entered Friday with the same record as the White Sox, but Chicago technically led the division because it holds the tiebreaker over Cleveland after winning the season series.
It means the Guardians must finish with more wins than the Sox to win the Central for a third straight year. Ramírez helped; his towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity.
Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez.
The home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered Friday with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery.
Ramírez has been dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. On Friday, he reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way.
